We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-10\lambda m+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-5\lambda )(m-5\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=5\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{5\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{5\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{5\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{5\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda x}+B{e}^{5\lambda x}+5B\lambda x{e}^{5\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ 5A\lambda +B+5B\lambda  & =0 \\ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{10\lambda }+2B{e}^{10\lambda }+2(5A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(5A\lambda +B+10B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+10A\lambda +2B+20B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+(4+20\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}5\lambda  & 1+5\lambda  \\ 1+10\lambda  & 4(1+5\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\lambda \cdot 4(1+5\lambda )-(1+5\lambda )(1+10\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -(1+10\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -1-10\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )(10\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}A{e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+2(6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+12A\lambda +2B+12B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+B=0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+12\lambda  & 3+12\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda  & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1).
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/92b9a6c83dd18a5599bbee71d714b26fddd62eb32917a5df983edc232664067b.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-{e}^{x}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}},\,-1\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x{y}^{2}-{e}^{x})\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy-2xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=x+y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=v$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y=1\,⟹\,v=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x-y=u$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y=1\,⟹\,u=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x+y=v$ and $x-y=u$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=2\,⟹\,(x-y)(x+y)=2,\,⟹\,uv=2.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(1,1).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}uv=2 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=2 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}uv=2 \\ u=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ v=2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(1,1),$ $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le \frac{2}{u}}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14111253/assets/4c151e7fc8d150b9c8def69d609446b77424c2703decd9c8c55866cff2ae7437.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(2)^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{2/u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}[v]_{1}^{2/u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{2}{u}-1)du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[2\operatorname{ln}⁡u-u]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-1) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′}=f(x,y,z)\, & z(a)=d,\end{aligned}
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y & =0 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =y-4{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{y-4{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=2.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(1)=-1, \\ {z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}},\, & z(1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=2.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=2$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=-1$ and $z(1)=2.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ |  |  | $2$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=2 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{-1-4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}}=-9 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=1 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=-9\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{9}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+1=0 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=2-\frac{9}{2}=-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{2}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=-\frac{5}{2} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{0-4(-\frac{5}{2})}{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{10}{(\frac{9}{4})}=\frac{40}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{40}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{20}{9} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0-\frac{5}{4}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{20}{9}=-\frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{40}{9}$ | $\frac{20}{9}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{18}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(2)≈-\frac{5}{4}$
and
${y}^{′}(2)=z(2)≈-\frac{5}{18}.$

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}6y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}6y\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}6y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,6y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$

Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

The area of the plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2}=8\pi .
$$

 

Since the mass is distributed uniformly, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{8\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }({\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }({\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}{|}_{0}^{4}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }\cdot 64\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =4M.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to find the minimum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=x-2y-2z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x+y+z=2,\,h(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=2 \\ h(x,y,z)=1\end{aligned}
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩+\mu ⟨2x,0,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda +2\mu x \\ -2=\lambda  \\ -2=\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{3}{2\mu } \\ \lambda =-2 \\ \mu z=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction. So, from the third equation above, we must have $z=0.$

Next, we substitute $z=0$  into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $z$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=1$ and $z=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\ 1+y+0 & =2 \\ 1+y & =2 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-1$ and $z=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\ -1+y+0 & =2 \\ -1+y & =2 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(1,1,0),\,(-1,3,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(1,1,0)$ | $(-1,3,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $-1$ | $-7$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-1,3,0),$ and its  minimum value is $-7.$

An indicator function maps elements from a set to the values $0$ or $1,$ depending on whether the element belongs to a specified subset. The indicator function is designed to "indicate" whether an element is a member of a subset.

More specifically, consider a universal set $X.$ Then, the indicator function of a set $A⊆X$ is the function

$$
{1}_{A}(x)={\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }x\in A, \\ 0, & \text{if }x\notin A.\end{aligned}
$$

The indicator function of the set ${2,4,8}$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14114807/assets/850019897d92b0a8d3340c091cee15342be20e99e7578a9fca23f88804e3bf28.png)

 

Notice that the elements $2,4$ and $8$ (the elements of our subset) are mapped to $1,$ and all other elements are mapped to $0.$

The residue class $[7]_{11}$ consists of the elements that are congruent to $7$ modulo $11.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[7]_{11} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡7\,(\text{mod}\,11)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x=7+11k,\,k\in Z} \\  & ={7+11k\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,\,7-2\cdot 11,\,7-11,\,7,\,7+11,\,7+2\cdot 11,…} \\  & ={…,-15,-4,7,18,29,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $-4$ and $18$ belong to $[7]_{11},$ while $15$ does not.

- *reflexive* if $(x,x)\in R$ for all $x\in A,$

- *irreflexive* if $(x,x)\notin R$ for all $x\in A.$

If some pairs of the form $(x,x)$ belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

In our case, the relation is defined on ${1,3,5,7},$ and we have

$$
(1,1)\notin R,\,(3,3)\notin R,\,(5,5)\notin R,\,(7,7)\notin R.
$$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

$\,$ Since $(x,x)\notin R$ $\text{for all }x\in A,$ the relation is $\text{irreflexive}.$

- *reflexive* if $(x,x)\in R$ for all $x\in A,$

- *irreflexive* if $(x,x)\notin R$ for all $x\in A.$

If some pairs of the form $(x,x)$ belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

In our case, the relation is defined on $\{5,8,10\},$ and we have

$$
(5,5)\in R,\,(8,8)\notin R,\,(10,10)\notin R.
$$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

$\,$ Since $(8,8)\notin R$ $\text{and }(5,5)\in R,$ the relation is $\text{neither reflexive nor irreflexive}.$

records.before:
Two sets $A$ and $B$ have the *same cardinality* if there exists a bijection between $A$ and $B.$

Notice that the elements of $B$ form an (infinite) arithmetic sequence with a common difference $d=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =-1 \\  & =6-7 \\  & =5-6 \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

The $n$th term of our arithmetic sequence, denoted ${b}_{n},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =7+(n-1)(-1) \\  & =7-n+1 \\  & =8-n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express $B$ in set-builder notation as 

$$
B={8-n∣\,n\in N}.
$$

Now, consider the function $f:A\to B$ that maps the underlying sets as follows: 

| $A$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $⋯$ | $n$ | $⋯$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $B$ | $7$ | $6$ | $5$ | $4$ | $⋯$ | $8-n$ | $⋯$ |

In general, for each $n\in A,$ we have $f(n)=8-n\in B.$

Notice that $f$ is described in such a way that it is bijective. Indeed, it's

- injective since $f(n)\ne f(m)$ whenever $n\ne m,$ and

- surjective since each element in $B$ (the second row) has a pre-image in $A$ (the first row).

Therefore, $|A|=|B|,$ i.e., the sets have the same cardinality.

First, we reorganize the equations so that they are in the right order, to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4x-2y=4 \\ 5x=6.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can represent this system of equations in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the solution, we need to calculate the inverse of the coefficient matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}].$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 0-5\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the solution to this system as:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- the *range* of $R$ is the set containing all elements from $B$ that appear as the second component of the ordered pairs in $R.$

$$

- Notice that $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)$ is continuous on $R,$ and has neither lower nor upper bounds. So, the set of second components contains all real numbers $R.$

If a relation $R$ is defined over $A={{a}_{1},{a}_{2},…,{a}_{m}}$ and $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},…{b}_{n}}$ of cardinalities $m$ and $n,$ respectively, the *adjacency matrix* of $R$ is a $m\times n$-matrix (or table), where the element ${r}_{ij}$ at the intersection of the $i$th row and the $j$th column is given by

$$
{r}_{ij}={\begin{aligned}1,\,\text{if }{a}_{i}\,R\,{b}_{j}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine the given ordered pairs.

- The pair $(✠,♣)$ belongs to the relation. Indeed, the adjacency matrix has $1$ on the intersection of the $✠$-row and the $♣$-column.

- The pair $(♣,♠)$ does not belong to the relation since the adjacency matrix has $0$ on the intersection of the $♣$-row and the $♠$-column.

- The pair $(♠,✠)$ does not belong to the relation since the adjacency matrix has $0$ on the intersection of the $♠$-row and the $✠$-column.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius $a=3$ and vertical radius $b=4.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which we can write as

$$
16{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=144.
$$

We're interested in describing all points that lie *inside* the ellipse. So, let's pick any point inside the region, say, $(0,0).$ Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

$$
16(0)^{2}+9(0)^{2}\,<\,144.
$$

As a result, the points $P(x,y)$ in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

$$

$$

Notice that we use $<$ since the boundary is excluded from the set (the boundary curve is dashed).

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$

$$

$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=2 \\ 3{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=2\end{aligned}
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -8 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -8 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -5 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=2 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=-5 \\ {x}_{3}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=6.$ Substituting ${x}_{3}=6$ into the second equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{2}-6=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1.
$$

Now, substituting ${x}_{2}=1$ and ${x}_{3}=6$ into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-3(1)+2(6)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-7.
$$

$$

$$

Consequently, 

$$

$$

The indicator function $1[P]$ equals $1$ if the predicate $P$ is true and $0$ if $P$ is false.

$$
1[P]={\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-5,$ we evaluate each indicator function:

- $1[x\ge 0]=1[-5\ge 0]=0$ (since $-5\ge 0$ is false)

- $1[-3\le x<0]=1[-3\le -5<0]=0$ (since $-3\le -5$ is false)

- $1[x<-3]=1[-5<-3]=1$ (since $-5<-3$ is true)

Substituting into the expression for $p(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(-5) & =0\cdot 25+0\cdot 1+1\cdot (-2(-5)) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the indicator functions act as a "switch": since $x=-5<-3,$ only the third term contributes to the result.

M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -6 & 10 \\ -1 & 3 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -6 & 10 \\ -1 & 3 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 5 \\ -1 & 3 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-3y=5 \\ 0x+0y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x-3y=5.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=5+3y,$ and the general solution is

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=5+3y \\ y=y\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5+3y \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,12,\,24,\,48,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =\frac{12}{6} \\  & =\frac{24}{12} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=6,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={3\cdot {2}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

$$
{-3,-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}}={x\in R\,:\,3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-45=0}.
$$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ {x}^{3}+y+1=0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the first equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0\,⇒\,y=-x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $y$ into the second equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+y+1 & =0 \\ {x}^{3}+(-x-1)+1 & =0 \\ {x}^{3}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x(x-1)(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =-1,\text{ }0,\text{ }1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $y:$

- For $x=0,$ we get $y=-0-1=-1.$

- For $x=1,$ we get $y=-1-1=-2.$

- For $x=-1,$ we get $y=-(-1)-1=0.$

Therefore, the equilibrium points are

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\text{and}\,[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$
